mainTopic: היזק שאינו ניכר and fining an accidental doer: מי חטאת, the robber who returns a ruined item, and how רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה apply fines
overview: The amud opens by settling a clash between a ברייתא, which says work with מי חטאת makes the water unfit, and רבא, who says water used in weighing stays fit. The גמרא's final answer is that both cases involve weighing against the water, and the water becomes unfit only if the person stopped paying attention to guarding it. רב פפא then brings a משנה: a robber whose stolen coin, תרומה or חמץ lost its value without any visible change may just return it. That refutes חזקיה's view that היזק שאינו ניכר counts as damage. The גמרא suggests that רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about this same question, in the case of someone who makes another person's food impure, mixes תרומה into it, or pours his wine for an idol. רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that everyone agrees unseen damage is not real damage. In his view, the argument is about whether the חכמים fined an accidental doer because of a deliberate one. That raises contradictions from the ברייתא about cooking on שבת. The גמרא resolves them with a split between rabbinic and Torah laws, and treats עבודה זרה as a special case for each תנא. A final contradiction from planting a tree in שביעית is answered by רבי מאיר's own special reason, that people count years from שביעית, and his explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבא's ruling that weighed water stays fit
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of a challenge: רבא ruled that מי חטאת used in weighing are still fit. That seems to contradict the ברייתא that work with the water disqualifies it.
steps.simpleTranslation: [But רבא said that מי חטאת] with which he weighed weights are fit!
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining a question the גמרא already started. It is pointing out that רבא said water used for weighing is still kosher, and that seems to clash with the ברייתא quoted just before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא implied that doing work with מי חטאת ruins them. Weighing things with the water sounds like doing work with it, yet רבא says the water stays fit. So the גמרא must explain how both statements can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: Purification water mixed with the ashes of the פרה אדומה

phrases.english: with which he weighed weights is fit!
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence that started just before: 'But רבא said, מי חטאת with which...'

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁשָּׁקַל בָּהֶן מִשְׁקָלוֹת, כְּשֵׁרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a challenge begun before this section
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that doing work with מי חטאת disqualifies them
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא rules that weighing with the water leaves it fit, so work does not seem to disqualify it.

steps.title: Weighing with the water versus weighing against it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא means using the water itself as part of the weighing, and רבא means putting it on the other side of the scale.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this case is with the water itself, and that case is against the water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by saying the two sources are talking about two different ways of weighing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the water itself is used to do the weighing, that is real work and disqualifies it, as the ברייתא says. If the water just sits opposite the object as a counterweight, that is not considered using the water, so רבא says it stays fit.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the formula for an answer
Opposite it, against it on a scale

phrases.english: It is not difficult: this is with the water itself,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the ברייתא, which says the water becomes unfit.

phrases.english: that is against the water.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּגוּפָן, הָא בִּכְנֶגְדָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source refers to a different method of weighing
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to describe the same act of weighing with the water
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא refers to weighing with the water itself, and רבא refers to weighing against it

steps.title: Real use of the water should make him liable in human court
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the answer: weighing with the water itself is a real act, and if unseen damage counts as damage, the person should be liable even in human court.
steps.simpleTranslation: With the water itself, he is doing a real act with it. And if damage that cannot be seen is called damage, he should be liable in human court too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks its own answer from step 2 and shows it does not fit with the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the person who does work with the water is free in human court and liable only before Heaven. Weighing with the water itself would be a real act, and according to the view that unseen damage counts as damage, a real act causing such damage should bring liability in human court. So the ברייתא cannot be talking about weighing with the water itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage that cannot be seen; the object looks the same but lost its value
Human court, where a court can force payment

phrases.english: With the water itself, he is doing an act with it;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק,
phrases.english: and if damage that cannot be seen is called damage,
he should be liable in human court too!

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּגוּפָן – מַעֲשֶׂה קָא עָבֵיד בְּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 2
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא refers to weighing with the water itself
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A real act causing damage that counts legally would bring liability in human court, but the ברייתא says he is free in human court.

steps.title: Both cases are weighing against the water; the difference is attention
steps.stepSummary: New answer: both sources describe weighing against the water. The ברייתא is a case where he stopped paying attention to guarding the water, and רבא's case is where he kept paying attention.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, both are against the water. It is not difficult: this case is where he took his mind off it, and that case is where he did not take his mind off it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its first answer and offers a new way to separate the two sources.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now neither case involves a real act with the water. What makes the water unfit in the ברייתא is היסח הדעת, the person stopped watching over the water while busy weighing. In רבא's case he stayed focused, so the water stays fit.

keyTerms.meaning: This one and that one, both cases
He took his mind off it, stopped paying attention

steps.confusionAlert: The water here is not ruined by any physical act. It becomes unfit only because the person stopped guarding it, so the 'damage' is not something you can see.

phrases.english: Rather, both this and that are against the water;
and it is not difficult: this is where he took his mind off it,
that is where he did not take his mind off it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בִּכְנֶגְדָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer of step 2, which step 3 rejected
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new split between the cases, based on attention instead of how the weighing was done
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference was weighing with the water versus against it
steps.terutzMaskana: Both cases are weighing against the water; disqualification depends on whether he took his mind off guarding it
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about מי חטאת is now read as weighing against the water while the person lost focus. That keeps him free in human court.

steps.title: רב פפא cites the case of a robber who returns a ruined item
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא brings a משנה: a robber who stole a coin that became invalid, תרומה that became impure, or חמץ that was kept over פסח can simply return it and say 'here is yours.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא objects: If someone robbed a coin and it became invalid, or תרומה and it became impure, or חמץ and פסח passed over it, he may say to the owner: 'Here is yours in front of you.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge begins. רב פפא quotes a משנה that he will use against the view that unseen damage counts as damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In all three cases the item looks exactly the same but has lost its value: the coin can't be spent, impure תרומה can't be eaten, and חמץ kept over פסח is forbidden. Still, the משנה lets the robber return the item as it is without paying for the loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Became invalid, here meaning the coin was taken out of use
Here is yours in front of you; returning the item as it is

phrases.english: Rav Pappa raises an objection:
If he robbed a coin, and it became invalid;
terumah, and it became impure;
leavened bread, and Pesach passed over it;
he says to him: 'Here is yours in front of you.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב רַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against the view that היזק שאינו ניכר counts as damage
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's view that היזק שאינו ניכר שמיה היזק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source text sets up a case of unseen damage where the robber is not required to pay; the attack is spelled out in the next step.

steps.title: If unseen damage counted, the robber would have to pay
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא spells out the challenge: if unseen damage counts as damage, the robber should have to pay full value, yet the משנה lets him return the item as it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say damage that cannot be seen is called damage, this man is a robber, so he should have to pay full, good money!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא applies the משנה to the question and shows it contradicts the view that unseen damage counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The damage to the coin, the תרומה and the חמץ is all unseen, because the items look unchanged. If such damage counted legally, the robber would have damaged the stolen item and would owe its full value. Since the משנה says 'here is yours' is enough, unseen damage must not count as damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Full, good money, meaning complete payment

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק,
phrases.english: And if you say damage that cannot be seen is called damage,
this one is a robber,
he should have to pay full money!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב פפא's objection by applying the משנה of step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's view that היזק שאינו ניכר שמיה היזק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under חזקיה's view, a robber who caused unseen damage would have to pay full value, but the משנה exempts him.

steps.title: The view that unseen damage counts is refuted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא declares this a תיובתא, a final refutation of חזקיה's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits there is no answer to רב פפא's objection, so the view that unseen damage counts as damage is rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A תיובתא means the objection stands and the view it attacked falls. From the robber case, the conclusion is that היזק שאינו ניכר does not count as damage for paying.

keyTerms.meaning: A final refutation; the challenged view is rejected

steps.whatToRemember: רב פפא's משנה proves that a robber can return an item whose loss of value cannot be seen. So the view that היזק שאינו ניכר שמיה היזק is refuted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule for the rest of the sugya: unseen damage is not treated as damage that must be paid for.

phrases.english: It is a refutation.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּיוּבְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes that רב פפא's objection cannot be answered
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: חזקיה's view that היזק שאינו ניכר שמיה היזק is refuted from the case of the robber who returns a ruined item.

steps.title: A ברייתא that may show תנאים argue about unseen damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that the argument about unseen damage is like an argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה. It quotes a ברייתא about someone who makes another person's food impure, mixes תרומה into it, or pours his wine for idol worship.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is an argument between תנאים. Someone who makes another person's food impure, mixes תרומה into his produce, or pours his wine for idol worship has to pay, whether he did it by accident or on purpose. That is רבי מאיר's view. רבי יהודה says: by accident, he is exempt; on purpose, he has to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to suggest that תנאים already argue about unseen damage. This step sets up the next line, which explains why the two opinions might be about that question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In all three cases the food or wine looks exactly the same, but it has lost value or become forbidden. That is unseen damage. רבי מאיר makes the person pay even for an accident, while רבי יהודה makes him pay only if he acted on purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: Like an argument between תנאים, the sages of the משנה era
One who makes something ritually impure
One who mixes תרומה into ordinary produce, so non-כהנים can no longer eat it
One who pours wine as an offering to an idol, making the wine forbidden
Doing something by accident or without knowing

phrases.english: Let us say it is like an argument between Tannaim:
One who makes impure, one who mixes in teruma, and one who pours as a libation,
whether by accident or on purpose, he is liable to pay,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
By accident, he is exempt; on purpose, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא כְּתַנָּאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After חזקיה's view was refuted, the גמרא looks for a תנאים argument behind the same question.
steps.raayaObject: That whether unseen damage counts as damage is argued by תנאים
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of הַמְטַמֵּא וְהַמְדַמֵּעַ וְהַמְנַסֵּךְ, with the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה

steps.title: Explaining the argument as being about unseen damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רבי מאיר holds unseen damage counts as damage, so even an accident requires payment. It suggests רבי יהודה holds it is not real damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this what they argue about? One sage holds that unseen damage is called damage, and the other sage holds that it is not called damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its suggestion. It says the argument in the ברייתא is about whether unseen damage counts as real damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If unseen damage is real damage, then like any damager you pay even for an accident. That fits רבי מאיר. If it is not real damage, payment is only a fine from the חכמים for someone who did it on purpose. That fits רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not...? This opens a suggested reading.

phrases.english: What, is it not about this that they argue?

phrases.aramaic: דְּמָר סָבַר: הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק;
phrases.english: One sage holds: damage that cannot be seen is called damage;
phrases.notes: This is רבי מאיר, who made even the accidental damager pay.

phrases.english: and the other sage holds: it is not called damage?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי, לָאו בְּהָא קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the ברייתא from step 8 in terms of the unseen-damage question.
steps.raayaObject: רבי מאיר holds unseen damage counts as damage, and רבי יהודה holds it does not
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי מאיר makes the accidental damager pay, while רבי יהודה exempts him

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: the argument is about fining accidents
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says everyone agrees unseen damage is not real damage. The real argument is whether the חכמים fined an accidental doer so that people would not do it on purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Everyone agrees that unseen damage is not called damage. Here they argue about whether the חכמים fined the accidental doer because of the deliberate doer. One sage holds they did fine him, and the other holds they did not.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק rejects the proof. He gives a different reason for the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that the payment is only a fine from the חכמים. רבי מאיר holds the fine was extended to accidents too, so people would not pretend they acted by mistake. רבי יהודה holds the fine applies only to someone who acted on purpose. So the ברייתא proves nothing about unseen damage.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים imposed a fine or penalty
The accidental doer because of the deliberate doer

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule of fining an accidental doer because of a deliberate one appears in many places in ש״ס. It is a common way to explain arguments about penalties from the חכמים.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר לָא שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק;
phrases.english: Everyone agrees that damage that cannot be seen is not called damage;

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכָא בְּקָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד קָא מִיפַּלְגִי –
phrases.english: and here they argue about whether they fined the accidental doer because of the deliberate doer.

phrases.aramaic: דְּמָר סָבַר: קָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד;
phrases.english: One sage holds: they fined the accidental doer because of the deliberate doer;

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: לֹא קָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד.
phrases.english: and the other sage holds: they did not fine the accidental doer because of the deliberate doer.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading in step 9 and gives a different reason for the argument.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתא shows תנאים arguing about unseen damage
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument can be explained another way: whether the fine also covers an accidental doer, with both sides agreeing that unseen damage is not real damage.

steps.title: Contradiction from food cooked on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that רב נחמן בר יצחק's explanation creates a contradiction. In the case of cooking on שבת, רבי מאיר does not penalize an accidental cook, while רבי יהודה does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now we can point out a contradiction between two statements of רבי מאיר, and between two statements of רבי יהודה. A ברייתא teaches: Someone who cooks on שבת by accident may eat the food; if on purpose, he may not eat it. That is רבי מאיר's view. רבי יהודה says: by accident, it may be eaten after שבת ends; on purpose, it may never be eaten.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק's explanation by bringing another ברייתא in which each תנא seems to hold the opposite view. The answer comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב נחמן בר יצחק, רבי מאיר fines accidents and רבי יהודה does not. But with cooking on שבת, רבי מאיר lets the accidental cook eat the food, so there is no fine. רבי יהודה makes him wait until after שבת, which is a fine. Each sage seems to contradict himself.

keyTerms.meaning: And one can point out a contradiction

steps.confusionAlert: The contradiction is not about unseen damage. It is about whether each sage fines an accidental doer, which is the reason רב נחמן בר יצחק just gave.

phrases.english: And one can point out a contradiction between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Meir,
and a contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yehuda,
as it was taught in a baraita: One who cooks on Shabbat:
if by accident, it may be eaten; if on purpose, it may not be eaten,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
if by accident, it may be eaten after Shabbat ends,
if on purpose, it may never be eaten.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָמֵי דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר אַדְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation of רב נחמן בר יצחק in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim that רבי מאיר fines accidents and רבי יהודה does not
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With cooking on שבת, רבי מאיר does not penalize the accidental cook, and רבי יהודה does make him wait. That is the opposite of what each holds in the ברייתא about impure food, mixed תרומה, and wine poured for an idol.

steps.title: The last opinion in the Shabbat ברייתא, and the double contradiction
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends with רבי יוחנן הסנדלר's opinion. Then the גמרא states it plainly: רבי מאיר seems to contradict himself, and so does רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן הסנדלר says: if he cooked by accident, the food may be eaten after שבת by other people, but not by him. If he cooked on purpose, it may never be eaten, not by him and not by others. So רבי מאיר contradicts רבי מאיר, and רבי יהודה contradicts רבי יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא about cooking on שבת and then says the problem out loud: each of the two תנאים seems to contradict himself. This sets up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier ברייתא (making food impure, mixing in תרומה, pouring wine for idols), רבי מאיר fines the accidental doer and רבי יהודה does not. In the שבת ברייתא it is the reverse: רבי מאיר lets the accidental cook eat, and רבי יהודה makes him wait until after שבת. Each one flips sides, so each has a contradiction to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a contradiction between one statement of this person and another statement of his

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוחנן הסנדלר's opinion is just the end of the ברייתא. The contradiction the גמרא is pointing to is only about רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan HaSandlar says:
If by accident, it may be eaten after Shabbat ends
by others, but not by him;
if on purpose, it may never be eaten
not by him, and not by others.
Rabbi Meir contradicts Rabbi Meir,
Rabbi Yehuda contradicts Rabbi Yehuda!

steps.triggerLanguage: קַשְׁיָא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר אַדְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר, קַשְׁיָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אַדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted in step 11 and states its contradiction openly
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's reading that רבי מאיר fines accidental doers and רבי יהודה does not
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the שבת cooking case each תנא holds the opposite of his position in the earlier ברייתא, so each contradicts himself

steps.title: רבי מאיר fines only for rabbinic laws
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר fines an accidental doer only when he broke a rabbinic law. For a Torah law, like cooking on שבת, he does not fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no contradiction in רבי מאיר. When he fines, it is for a rabbinic law. For a Torah law he does not fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction in רבי מאיר by splitting the cases into rabbinic laws and Torah laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making food impure is only a rabbinic problem, so רבי מאיר adds a fine even for accidents, so that people won't come to do it on purpose. Cooking on שבת is a Torah law, and people already take Torah laws seriously, so no extra fine is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A law made by the חכמים

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר אַדְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר לָא קַשְׁיָא –
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir against Rabbi Meir is not a difficulty
when he fines, it is for a rabbinic law;
for a Torah law he does not fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר אַדְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first half of the contradiction from step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (rabbinic law vs. Torah law)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר always fines accidental doers
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר fines accidental doers only for rabbinic laws

steps.title: But pouring wine for idols is a Torah law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: pouring wine for idols is forbidden by the Torah, yet רבי מאיר fines for it even by accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: But pouring wine for idols is a Torah law, and he does fine for it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer just given for רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי מאיר does not fine for Torah laws, why does he fine the accidental pourer of wine for idols in the earlier ברייתא? That case does not fit the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who pours wine as an offering to an idol

phrases.english: But pouring wine for idols is a Torah law,
and he does fine!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא מְנַסֵּךְ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא הוּא, וְקָא קָנֵיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer in step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that רבי מאיר does not fine for Torah laws
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The pouring of wine for idols is a Torah law, yet רבי מאיר fines for it

steps.title: עבודה זרה is a special case for רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: Because עבודה זרה is so severe, רבי מאיר fines for it even though it is a Torah law.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because עבודה זרה is so severe, he fines him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that עבודה זרה is an exception to רבי מאיר's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule stays the same: no fine for accidental Torah sins. עבודה זרה is so serious that רבי מאיר makes an exception and fines even here.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר: fine an accidental sinner for rabbinic laws, not for Torah laws, except עבודה זרה, which is so severe that he fines there too.

phrases.english: Because of the severity of idol worship,
he fines him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם חוּמְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, קָנֵס לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 14
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pouring wine for idols should follow the Torah-law rule and get no fine
steps.terutzMaskana: עבודה זרה is so severe that רבי מאיר fines for it anyway

steps.title: רבי יהודה fines only for Torah laws
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה does not fine an accidental doer for a rabbinic law, but he does fine for a Torah law like cooking on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no contradiction in רבי יהודה. When he does not fine, it is for a rabbinic law. For a Torah law he does fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now answers the second contradiction, about רבי יהודה, with the same split but in the opposite direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, a Torah law is so serious that even an accident deserves a fine, so the accidental cook must wait until after שבת. A rabbinic law is lighter, so he does not fine an accident there.
steps.confusionAlert: Both תנאים use the same split (rabbinic vs. Torah), but they reach opposite results. רבי מאיר fines the lighter law; רבי יהודה fines the heavier one.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אַדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה לָא קַשְׁיָא –
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda against Rabbi Yehuda is not a difficulty
when he does not fine, it is for a rabbinic law;
for a Torah law he fines.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אַדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second half of the contradiction from step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (rabbinic law vs. Torah law)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהודה never fines accidental doers
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה fines accidental doers only for Torah laws

steps.title: But pouring wine for idols is a Torah law, and רבי יהודה does not fine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: pouring wine for idols is a Torah law, yet רבי יהודה does not fine the accidental doer.
steps.simpleTranslation: But pouring wine for idols is a Torah law, and he does not fine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer just given for רבי יהודה, using the same case as before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי יהודה fines for Torah laws, he should fine the accidental pourer of wine for idols. But in the earlier ברייתא he does not.

phrases.english: But pouring wine for idols is a Torah law,
and he does not fine!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא מְנַסֵּךְ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, וְלָא קָנֵיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer in step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that רבי יהודה fines for Torah laws
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Pouring wine for idols is a Torah law, yet רבי יהודה does not fine for it

steps.title: People already stay far from עבודה זרה
steps.stepSummary: Because עבודה זרה is so severe, people keep away from it on their own, so רבי יהודה sees no need for a fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because עבודה זרה is so severe, people keep themselves far away from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that עבודה זרה is an exception for רבי יהודה too, but for the opposite reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same severity that made רבי מאיר fine makes רבי יהודה not fine. Since everyone already keeps far from idol worship, a fine is not needed to keep people away from it.

keyTerms.meaning: They keep themselves far away from it

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה: fine an accidental sinner for Torah laws, not for rabbinic laws, except עבודה זרה, where people already stay away on their own. The severity of עבודה זרה cuts both ways.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how one fact, the severity of עבודה זרה, can be used as a reason for opposite results, depending on why the fine exists.

phrases.english: Because of the severity of idol worship,
people keep themselves far from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם חוּמְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה. מִיבְדָּל בְּדִילִי מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 17, flipping the reasoning of step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exception because of severity (people avoid it by themselves)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pouring wine for idols should follow the Torah-law rule and get a fine
steps.terutzMaskana: People already avoid עבודה זרה, so רבי יהודה does not fine for it

steps.title: רבי מאיר seems to fine an accidental planter in the seventh year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא where רבי מאיר says a tree planted in שביעית must be uprooted even if it was planted by accident. This seems to clash with his ruling that an accidental cook on שבת is not fined.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you can set רבי מאיר against רבי מאיר even about a Torah law. A ברייתא teaches: if someone plants on שבת by accident, he may keep the tree. If he did it on purpose, he must uproot it. If he plants during שביעית, he must uproot it whether he did it by accident or on purpose. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי מאיר again. Here he fines an accidental planter in שביעית, even though שביעית is a Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי מאיר did not fine someone who cooked on שבת by accident, a Torah law. Planting in שביעית is also a Torah law, yet here he fines even the accidental planter. So his approach to Torah laws looks inconsistent.

keyTerms.meaning: And one can raise a contradiction (literally: 'and he throws' one source against another)
A law from the Torah itself
The seventh year (שמיטה), when working the land is forbidden
He may keep it (the tree stays)

phrases.english: But one can contrast Rabbi Meir against Rabbi Meir
even regarding a Torah law
as it was taught: One who plants on Shabbat,
if by accident, he may keep it;
if on purpose, he must uproot it;

phrases.aramaic: וּבַשְּׁבִיעִית – בֵּין בְּשׁוֹגֵג בֵּין בְּמֵזִיד יַעֲקֹר,
phrases.english: and in the seventh year, whether by accident or on purpose, he must uproot it,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָמֵי דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר אַדְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר בִּדְאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction from step 13 by showing רבי מאיר fines an accidental planter in שביעית, which is a Torah law.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 13 that רבי מאיר does not fine an accidental doer for a Torah law.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Planting in שביעית is also a Torah law, yet רבי מאיר fines even the accidental planter, so his rule on Torah laws seems inconsistent.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's opposite ruling in the same ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: רבי יהודה lets an accidental planter in שביעית keep the tree, but on שבת the tree must be uprooted either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: in שביעית, if he planted by accident he may keep the tree, and if on purpose he must uproot it. On שבת, whether by accident or on purpose, he must uproot it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes by quoting רבי יהודה, who flips רבי מאיר's ruling. This sets up the גמרא's next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה is strict about שבת and lenient about an accidental planter in שביעית. That is the exact reverse of רבי מאיר, even though both laws come from the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: Doing something by accident or without knowing
Whether... or... (both cases are the same)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
in the seventh year, if by accident, he may keep it,
if on purpose, he must uproot it;

phrases.aramaic: וּבַשַּׁבָּת – בֵּין בְּשׁוֹגֵג בֵּין בְּמֵזִיד, יַעֲקֹר.
phrases.english: and on Shabbat, whether by accident or on purpose, he must uproot it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בַּשְּׁבִיעִית – בְּשׁוֹגֵג יְקַיֵּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא quoted in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, an accidental planter in שביעית keeps the tree, but on שבת the tree is uprooted either way.

steps.title: The ברייתא itself treats two Torah laws differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: if this is a problem, the ברייתא is already a problem on its own. שבת and שביעית are both Torah laws, yet both תנאים treat them differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: And by your reasoning, the ברייתא itself should bother you. After all, this is a Torah law and that is a Torah law, so what is different about שבת and what is different about שביעית?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a counter-question. It shows that the ברייתא must have a special reason for treating שבת and שביעית differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both תנאים split between שבת and שביעית, even though both are Torah laws. So the split cannot be about 'Torah law versus rabbinic law.' There must be some other reason specific to these cases, and that weakens the contradiction.

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning,
the source itself should be difficult for you:
phrases.notes: 'The source itself' means the ברייתא about planting that was just quoted.

phrases.english: after all, this is a Torah law
and that is a Torah law,
what is different about Shabbat
and what is different about the seventh year?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְטַעְמָיךְ, תִּקָּשֶׁה לָךְ הִיא גּוּפַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes back against the contradiction raised in step 19 by pointing to the ברייתא's own split.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the assumption that this ברייתא is following a general rule about Torah laws.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא treats two Torah laws differently, so some reason specific to these cases must be at work. That makes the comparison to cooking on שבת invalid.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's own reason: people count years from the seventh year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the ברייתא gives its own reason. רבי מאיר explains that he is stricter with שביעית because the Jewish people count years by the שביעית cycle.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, in that case, the reason is as it is taught. רבי מאיר said: Why do I say that on שבת, by accident he may keep the tree and on purpose he must uproot it, but in שביעית he must uproot it either way? Because the Jewish people count from the seventh year...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the problem. The ruling about planting has its own special reason, which רבי מאיר states himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fine in שביעית is not about whether the law comes from the Torah. It comes from something special about שביעית: people count the years by it. So it does not clash with his lenient ruling about cooking on שבת. רבי מאיר's explanation continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: As the reason is taught (the source itself gives the reason)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר's strictness about planting in שביעית is not a general rule about Torah laws. It comes from a reason specific to שביעית, so there is no real contradiction with his ruling on cooking on שבת.

phrases.english: Rather, there, it is as the reason is taught:
Rabbi Meir said:
For what reason do I say
that on Shabbat, if by accident, he may keep it,
if on purpose, he must uproot it;

phrases.aramaic: וּבַשְּׁבִיעִית – בֵּין בְּשׁוֹגֵג בֵּין בְּמֵזִיד יַעֲקֹר?
phrases.english: but in the seventh year, whether by accident or on purpose, he must uproot it?
Because the Jewish people count from the seventh year,
phrases.notes: The sentence is not finished here. רבי מאיר's explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָתָם, כִּדְקָתָנֵי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the special reason that step 21 showed must exist.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing reason stated explicitly in the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר seems to fine accidental Torah violations in שביעית, which would contradict his ruling about cooking on שבת.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fine in שביעית rests on a reason specific to שביעית: people count years from it. It is not a general policy about Torah laws.
